pedagogy.summary: At ages 7–8 this topic is about sorting familiar Earth events onto a fast↔slow timescale using evidence — earthquakes and volcanic eruptions happen in seconds to days, while erosion, canyon-carving and mountain-building take an unimaginably long time. It is taught qualitatively (no measured timescales), using dramatic before/after images and time-lapse video to make slow changes visible, and by having children gather evidence from several sources (text, images, video) to justify each classification.
bestPractices: Contrast concrete, familiar examples at each end — an earthquake or eruption (fast) against erosion, a carved canyon or a rising mountain (slow) — rather than defining the categories abstractly.
Make slow change visible with time-lapse video and before/after image pairs, since children cannot directly observe processes longer than a lifetime.
Keep it qualitative — sort as fast vs slow, do NOT quantify timescales (matching the assessment boundary).
Have children cite evidence from several sources to support the distinction, building the practice of an evidence-based account.
Address the intuition that land is permanent — use paired images showing the same place changing — and that all geological change is gradual.
Connect to lived experience (a landslide or flood on the news vs a weathered old wall) to anchor the timescale idea.
keyRepresentations: A fast↔slow timescale line (seconds → millions of years) with events placed along it.
Before/after image pairs of the same landscape (a cliff collapse; a slowly widening canyon).
Time-lapse clips compressing slow processes into seconds.
A two-column sort: rapid events vs slow processes.
commonMisconceptions: All changes to the land are slow and gradual — or, conversely, that landscapes are permanent and never change.
Fast events (earthquakes) and slow processes (erosion) are the same kind of thing.
Mountains, canyons and coastlines have 'always been there' as they are now.
Slow processes are not really happening because you cannot see them move.

learn.summary: For ages 7–8, help children sort familiar Earth events onto a fast↔slow timescale using evidence, without quantifying the timescales. Fast events (earthquakes, volcanic eruptions) cause big changes within seconds to days that people can watch happen, though some eruptions continue on and off for months or years. Slow processes (erosion, canyon carving, mountain building) take far longer than a lifetime to make big changes, even if small bits of wearing-away can sometimes be seen. Make slow change believable with before/after image pairs and time-lapse, and have children justify each classification from several sources (text, images, video). The target insight is that 'the land changes' and 'the land changes slowly' are both true.

activities.title: Drag-and-play fast↔slow timescale line
feedback: If a child places the canyon near the fast end, ask: 'Could you stand and watch the canyon get deeper the way you could watch a volcano erupt? Why not?' and show time-lapse of a river slowly cutting rock.

If a child says the canyon was cut quickly in one big flood, acknowledge that very big floods can carve some small gorges quickly, but contrast that with a large canyon like the Grand Canyon, cut by river water and floods repeated over and over for an unimaginably long time.
Praise a correct sort that gives a reason tied to whether the whole change could be watched happening, not just how dramatic it looks.
activities.rationale: An interactive timeline with time-lapse playback is intended to let children feel the contrast of timescales that the standard targets and to classify events with evidence. The dragging, play control and 'millions of years' dial are optional ways to make the slow-vs-fast mechanism concrete; a simpler paper line with cards works too. Because a slow process cannot be shown in real time, present the playback as a compressed time-lapse analogy. Keep it qualitative — sort fast vs slow without stating measured durations.

learnerActions: Place each Earth event (earthquake, volcanic eruption, river carving a canyon, a rising mountain, a cliff slowly worn back by waves) onto a line labelled from 'seconds' at one end to 'millions of years' at the other.

Play each event: a fast event like an earthquake is shown at about real speed and jolts the ground almost at once, while a slow one like a canyon deepening only becomes visible after you scrub a 'millions of years' control and watch the river do its slow work — this is a sped-up, compressed model of the slow process, not real time.
Put an earthquake and a canyon side by side on the line and describe, in your own words, how they are at opposite ends.

For each event you called 'slow', name a piece of evidence (rock layers built up over time, worn stone, a time-lapse made from real photos of a cliff or riverbank) that shows the change happens gradually over a long time; remember the sped-up canyon animation is a model, not evidence by itself.
activities.intendedInsight: Both fast events and slow processes reshape the land, but fast ones make big changes in moments to days while slow ones take far longer than a lifetime; being unable to watch a whole change happen does not mean it is not happening.

activities.title: Before/after detective with a tappable landscape
feedback: If a child insists a feature 'has always been there exactly like that', show the before/after pair for that same place and point out what differs.
When a child notices a difference and links it to how long the change would take, confirm and connect to a real example (a landslide on the news vs a weathered old wall).
activities.rationale: Tappable before/after pairs are developmentally approachable for this age and are intended to address the intuition that land is permanent. A fixed set of image pairs can introduce the idea, but on its own it does not let a child watch a slow transformation unfold; pair it with time-lapse so slow change is believable.
sourceClaims: A common student intuition is that landscapes are static/permanent or that all geological change is slow; making slow change visible (before/after, time-lapse) is a documented teaching need.
learnerActions: Explore a landscape and tap features — a volcano erupting, a fault that slipped during an earthquake, a canyon, a cliff slowly worn back by waves — to reveal whether each change was fast or slow along with a before/after image pair (photos for quick changes; drawings or reconstructions for changes too slow to photograph).
For each feature, say out loud what is different between the 'before' and 'after' pictures.
Decide whether that change could happen quickly or only over a very long time, and explain how you decided.
activities.intendedInsight: Paired images of the same place show that landscapes are not permanent; some features changed quickly and others changed over a time far longer than a lifetime.

activities.title: Evidence-based sort and sequence
feedback: If a child lists only dramatic events as 'changes' and omits erosion, show worn stone steps and an old gravestone or wall whose carved letters have faded as evidence that slow wearing-away is still change.
If a child sorts by drama (e.g. calls a canyon fast because it looks big), redirect to the observability test: could you watch the whole change happen from start to finish?
Reinforce sorts that are justified by cited evidence rather than by guessing.
activities.rationale: Categorising, sequencing and transferring to a new event is intended to check the fast/slow criterion and the practice of an evidence-based account. Sorting plus self-generated examples asks for construction, not only recognition. Keep it qualitative to match the assessment boundary.

learnerActions: Sort a set of events into two columns: rapid events vs slow processes.
Give at least two examples of your own for each column (e.g. earthquake, volcanic eruption, landslide, flood for fast; erosion, mountain formation, canyon carving for slow).
Order the events by roughly how long they take, from quickest to slowest, without stating exact times.
For the slow processes, point to evidence (rock strata, worn rock, a time-lapse made from real photos) that shows the change is real; a sped-up animation is a model, not evidence by itself.
Apply the rule to a brand-new event you have not seen before: fast or slow, and how do you know?
activities.intendedInsight: A useful test for 'fast or slow' is whether the whole change could be watched happening from start to finish, not how dramatic it looks; evidence can support a slow process even when you cannot see it move.

constraints: Keep the work qualitative: sort as fast vs slow and sequence roughly, but do NOT ask children to quantify timescales with measured numbers (matches the assessment boundary).
Playback of a slow process is always a compressed time-lapse, not real time; present it as such so children do not infer the simulation runs at literal true speed.
Before/after image sets and tappable reveals introduce the idea but cannot by themselves show a slow transformation unfolding; combine with time-lapse so a 'slow' change is believable.

A recognition sort or multiple-choice check assesses classification but does not by itself elicit the child independently generating examples or citing evidence; include tasks where children produce their own examples and reasons.
Anchor categories in concrete, familiar examples at each end rather than abstract definitions; connect to lived experience (news footage vs a weathered wall).
Judge fast vs slow by whether the whole change could be watched happening from start to finish, not by how dramatic it looks.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and efficacy wording is kept conditional (intended/proposed).
The third listed source (static/permanent landscape misconception) is marked verified:false in the row; treat the 'documented teaching need' framing as unverified.

The source row rated a 3D morphing landscape as 'possible but not spatially necessary' and dialogue/conversation as a poor fit for this sorting task; these are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws. A 3D time-lapse or a brief spoken discussion could still support this topic. These framings were softened or dropped rather than propagated as universal claims.

The 'true speed' playback in the original recommendation is necessarily a compressed/relative representation — a canyon cannot literally play in real time; the activity now presents it as a time-lapse analogy rather than literal real-time speed.

probeDeeper: Could you stand and watch the canyon get deeper the way you could watch a volcano erupt? Why not?
What evidence would show you that this land used to look different?
My cousin says mountains have always been exactly that shape. What could you tell him?
assess.correctAnswer: The volcanic eruption is the quick change (you could watch it happen in hours or days); the river carving the canyon is the slow change (it takes far longer than anyone could watch — many thousands or millions of years). The test is whether you could see the change happening.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'canyons and mountains have always looked like that — the land doesn't really change' (static-Earth, no deep time)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show layered or time-lapse evidence that land is always slowly changing — worn steps, a shrinking cliff, canyon strata — change too slow to watch is still change.
errorPatterns.distractor: The canyon has always been there, exactly as it is now.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: treats the present landscape as permanent; denies slow processes reshape land

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the river cut the canyon quickly, in one big flood' (catastrophist single-event thinking)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish a one-off fast event from a process repeated over vast time — a little water, over and over, for an unimaginably long time.
errorPatterns.distractor: A river cut the whole canyon in a single big flood.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: assigns a slow process to one dramatic fast event

errorPatterns.pattern: 'only earthquakes and volcanoes really change the land — slow wearing-away doesn't count' (dismisses gradual processes)
errorPatterns.nextMove: A rusting gate and worn stone steps show slow change is still change; gather evidence of gradual wearing over time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: lists only dramatic events as 'changes' and omits erosion/weathering

responseLevels.gap: Treats the landscape as permanent, or reverses fast/slow (canyon fast; mountains unchanging).
responseLevels.full: Classifies events as quick vs slow by whether the change could be observed happening, gives two of each, and cites evidence (strata, worn rock, video) for the slow ones; transfers to a new event.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts one or two events correctly but by how dramatic they are rather than by whether the change could be watched; cannot give evidence.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A river carves a deep canyon, and a volcano erupts. One of these changes the land quickly and one very slowly. Which is which — and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'dramatic = fast' or holds a static-Earth view answers by drama or says the canyon was cut quickly. A child reasoning correctly sorts events by whether the change could be observed happening, and can name evidence for the slow ones. The reason tier separates a genuine fast/slow criterion from a guess.
